[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#2/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The second min can be partitive, as 35:27 supports: not all water descends, not all fruit grows by rain, and not all sustenance consists of fruit; or it can explain the kind, with rizq meaning the provision received. | mentions 35:27
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#2/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Thamarāt can denote groups of individual fruits as a collective plural; the singular reading al-thamarah supports this explanation. [BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#3/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Lakum modifies rizq if it means the provision received; if rizq is a verbal noun, lakum is its object, meaning provision for you.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#3/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Fa-lā tajʿalū may coordinate a prohibition with worship, be subjunctive after an implied an, or depend on laʿalla so the sense is if you are mindful, do not make rivals; it may also be a prohibitive predicate of alladhī jaʿala. | mentions 40:36
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#3/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The causal fāʾ links the prohibition to God's having singled people out for immense blessings and signs: the One who granted them should not be associated with.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#3/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | A nidd is an opposing equal or likeness; the word is reserved for a counterpart matching in essence, while a like in degree is called a musāwī. Jarīr's verse uses nidd for a rival.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#3/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Calling idols rivals is sarcastic censure: polytheists need not claim equality with God in essence or attributes, but worshiping and naming them gods resembles believing they are self-existent and can repel harm or grant good.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#3/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · زيد بن عمرو بن نفيل | reports | The pre-Islamic monotheist Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl's verse contrasts worshiping one God with a thousand and declares that he abandoned al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#4/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Wa-antum taʿlamūn is circumstantial to the subject of fa-lā tajʿalū, with its object omitted: you are people of knowledge, reflection, and sound judgment.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#4/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, the omitted object is that idols neither resemble God nor can do what He does, as 30:40 asks whether partners can do any such thing; the point is rebuke, not restricting the duty to the learned. | mentions 30:40
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#4/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The two verses command worship and forbid associating partners, then give their rationale: lordship grounds worship; God created people, their ancestors, and necessities of life, and these uniquely divine provisions witness His oneness.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#4/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The verse can also allude to human formation: body is earth, soul heaven, intellect water, and practical and theoretical virtues produced through intellect and senses are fruits of joined celestial active and earthly receptive powers.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alladhī may be a second adjective, an accusative or nominative expression of praise, or a subject whose predicate is the prohibition fa-lā tajʿalū; jaʿala itself can mean become or begin intransitively, bring into being with one object, or render with two. | mentions 6:1
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Earth is made like a spread bed because some of it was raised above the enveloping water and balanced between hardness and softness, making it suitable for sitting and sleeping; this does not require a flat rather than spherical earth.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Jaʿala means ‘made’ or ‘rendered.’
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Thamarāt is used instead of thamar or thimār because the intended sense is a collection of fruits and plural forms interchange where both indicate collectivity.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r11] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Lakum modifies rizq if rizq means the provision itself; if it means the act of providing, it is an object, ‘providing you.’
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r12] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The prohibition follows the command to worship: tawḥīd is the basis of worship, so no equal or partner may be assigned to God.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r13] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Alternatively, alladhī is a subject whose predicate is the prohibition; the fāʾ introduces the consequence implicit in the discourse: since God surrounded them with signs, they should not take partners.

[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r15] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | The audience knows idols neither create nor provide while God is creator and provider; alternatively, the object of ‘know’ is omitted, meaning they are people of knowledge and idolatry is utter ignorance.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Alladhī may be accusative as a praise construction or nominative as the subject of an understood huwa.

[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Calling earth a spread does not prove it flat rather than spherical, since spreading and resting on it are possible on either account.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The sky is a roof; bināʾ is a verbal noun used for the built structure. He links this to 21:32. | mentions 2, 1, :, 3, 2
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The water sent down from the sky is rain.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Fruits emerge through God’s power, will, and creation; He makes water a cause, like reproductive fluid in a child’s creation, though He can create without causes, which He created along with matter.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Creating things gradually through successive states and stages contains wisdom and lessons for observers with insight.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Min is partitive or explanatory; rizqan is a purpose object with the partitive reading and a direct object of akhraja with the explanatory reading.
[QASHANI:2:21-22#2/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Islam requires both testimonies: unity alone hides differentiation and becomes determinism leading to heresy and antinomianism, while attributing acts only to the Messenger hides unity and becomes dualism; Islam joins both and regards the Messenger as the manifestation of divine acts.
[QASHANI:2:21-22#2/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Created acts relate to divine acts as body to spirit: spirit is their source but acts through the body, just as God originates acts that appear through creatures.
[QASHANI:2:21-22#2/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | A messenger is necessary because veiled, distant creatures cannot receive divine knowledge directly; a mediator combines a spirit witnessing the divine presence with a human nature among people, receives divine words, and conveys them to people who accept him through shared nature.
[QASHANI:2:21-22#2/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The Messenger receives the divine words in his heart and conveys them through his purified self to humankind.
[QASHANI:2:21-22/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The listed acts establish that only their maker deserves worship; knowingly attributing an act to another makes that other seem a rival worthy of worship.
[QASHANI:2:21-22/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Worshippers worship the maker, whose manifestation appears in created form; each knows God only to the extent of the divinity found within, and these people found only the voluntary agent.
[QASHANI:2:21-22/r7] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | In the inward analogy, souls are earth, spirits are sky, knowledge of unity of acts is rain, and surrender, obedience, good works, and virtues are the resulting growth that yields certainties, states, and stations such as patience, gratitude, and reliance.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p151#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Firāsh is a spread or bedding one sits, sleeps, and moves upon.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p151#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Bināʾ is a verbal noun but can mean a transported dwelling such as a house, dome, tent, or canopy; Arab abniya are tents.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p151#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Water is familiar; one account calls it a flowing substance that sustains animal life, and the supplied fragment cuts off during the further description.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The morphology of ماء is related to فعل, with its alif from wāw and hamza replacing hāʾ, as مويه، مياه، أمواه indicate.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | ثمره is what a tree produces that is edible or fragrant.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A ند is a resisting counterpart or peer, whether similar, opposite, or otherwise different.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة والمفضل | reports | Abu Ubayda and al-Mufaddal define ند as an opposite; Ibn Atiyya says this restriction is illustrative, not exhaustive.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · غيره | reports | Another authority defines ند as a hostile opposite that resists, deriving the word from flight.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المهدوي | reports | Al-Mahdawi defines ند as an equal or counterpart, the position of the linguists other than Abu Ubayda.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari says ند means an equal, used only for a counterpart that differs from the Creator.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · جرير | reports | Jarir's verse uses نديد for an equal counterpart, evidence for the sense of ند.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p152/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Saying God has neither ند nor ضد denies both anything that can take His place and anything opposed to Him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p156#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The relative الذي جعل can be nominative or accusative; the nominative analyses continue in the next segment.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | An adjective may itself be modified only when it cannot agree directly with its described noun; the example is يا أيها الفارس ذو الجمة.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The article on الأرض may designate prepared, level parts suitable as a bed, or all earth as a place for animals to settle and dwell.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | On the universal reading, lowlands, mountains, houses, and animal or bird shelters make earth a resting place; it is a favor to creatures or to people through animals prepared for their use.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abu al-Hasan permits a repeated-subject construction using a person's alternate name; Abū Ḥayyān says Sibawayh disallows it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | The accusative can detach as praise or describe ربكم, the referent of الذي خلقكم; he prefers adjectives to modify the same noun unless impossible.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مكي | reports | Abu Muhammad Makki allows the accusative by supplying أعني, but Abū Ḥayyān says the prior expression is unambiguous and needs no insertion.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مكي | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān calls Makki's further proposal to govern الذي by تتقون a gross parsing unworthy of the Qur'an.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The absence of a coordinating wāw before الذي keeps this and the prior description attached to one referent; conjunction would suggest a different referent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | جعل means “made into,” taking الأرض and فراشا as two objects, with لكم attached to جعل.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعضهم | reports | Others parse فراشا and بناء as circumstantial accusatives, treating جعل as “created” with one object and varying the verb for eloquence, as in 6:1. | mentions 6:1
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu Amr assimilates the lām of جعل into the lām of لكم.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · طلحة | reports | Talha reads مهادا; the segment continues his reading from the previous segment.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says the sky is called a building because its parts hold together like a building.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Fراش, مهاد, بساط, قرار, and وطأ are near-synonyms.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض المنجمين | reports | Some astronomers infer that earth is flat rather than spherical from its being made like a bed, and argue seas could not remain on a sphere.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects the inference: the verse describes earth's use as a bed but establishes neither a flat nor spherical shape; its vast size permits that use either way.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari argues that if people can spread bedding on a mountain, itself an earthly peg, they can do so more easily on broad earth.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قائلون | reports | The reply to the sea argument is that a sphere may have a level region for water, held by God's command rather than physical theory.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A stationary sphere could hold water on part of its surface; on a rotating sphere, water would ordinarily be unable to stay fixed, an issue for astronomy.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس وجماعة | reports | The sky is compared to a built dome over earth, as a house's roof is a construction; Ibn Abbas and others report this explanation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p158/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Calling the sky a building conveys firmness, craft, and protection, displaying divine power and wisdom: despi

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p159/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | God wisely brings things through successive stages; witnessing wondrous change and gradual development increases the observer's reverence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p159/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | من is partitive, the article marks a generic category, and the plural ثمرات reflects the diversity of types; there is no need to treat it as a substitute for ثمر or ثمار.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p159/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari treats الثمرات as a plural standing for the collective singular ثمر or plural ثمار; Abū Ḥayyān says the generic definite plural already covers the category.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p159/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | He notes that grammarians refuted criticism of Hassan's use of a definite low-count plural, since the definite article makes it exhaustive.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p160/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | من is not extra: grammarians do not otherwise allow it in affirmative constructions, and an exhaustive reading wrongly makes every fruit provision; partitive force fits the facts.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p160/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Indefinite water, partitive fruit, and indefinite provision fit partial benefits: some water produces some fruits, and only some provision consists of fruit.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p160/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | من الثمرات may be أخرج's object with رزقا circumstantial or a purpose complement; alternatively it attaches to أخرج and رزقا is its object.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p160/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن السميفع | reports | Ibn al-Sumayfa reads من الثمرة in the singular, using الثمرة collectively for fruits, like speaking of a garden's fruit or a poem's word.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p160/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | If رزق is a verbal noun, the kaf is its object with the lām understood; if it means provisioned goods, لكم modifies omitted كائنا, or attaches to أخرج.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p160/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The passage gives five signs: creating the addressees and their forebears, then earth as a bed, heaven as a building, and rain and fruit; humans come first as familiar, earth before sky, and effects after causes.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p160/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation puts accountable humans first because life, ability, desire, and reason are prerequisites for benefiting from the heavens, earth, water, and fruit.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p160/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · من قال السماء أفضل | reports | Those who consider the heavens superior cite the angels' worship there and the absence of any place where God was disobeyed; the excerpt starts citing Adam after his disobedience but ends before the quotation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | One case for heaven's superiority points to its precedence over earth in many verses, its Throne, Footstool, Preserved Tablet and Pen, and its being the direction of supplication.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He also objects that this parsing makes human creation serve the purpose of fearing punishment, which follows al-Zamakhshari's previously discussed Muʿtazilite doctrine.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another possible parse connects the prohibition to الذي, treated as the predicate of an omitted subject: he is the one who made these signs, so do not set up rivals.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · من قال الأرض أفضل | reports | Those preferring earth argue that God blessed places on it, prophets were made from it, and it serves as mosque and purifier.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Calling idols rivals is figurative: people share divinity's name and an outward form of worship with God, but resemble him only in that specified respect.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The polytheists worshipped idols to draw near to God, while calling him the god of gods and lord of lords; they did not worship idols for themselves.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The plural prohibition matches their actual practice of assigning God many rivals; Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl's poem asks whether one or a thousand lords should be worshipped.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · زيد بن علي بن محمد بن السميفع | reports | Zayd ibn Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa read ند in the singular; under negation it is generic, not a command to avoid only one rival.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | The prohibition most naturally attaches to the command to worship the Lord: worship entails affirming God's unity and devoting worship to him alone.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari attaches the prohibition to لعل, parses تجعلوا as subjunctive after a hope, and understands creation as aimed at fear of God's punishment.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan rejects al-Zamakhshari's parsing because Basran grammarians do not allow a subjunctive as the answer to hope; only Kufans analogize it to an interrogative answer.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The clause is circumstantial; its omitted object is deliberate, since the point is to establish that the addressees possess knowledge and discernment, making idolatry especially unfit for them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو محمد ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya says God's blessings suffice people without any creature; one who makes himself dependent on another through greed, hope or worldly desire takes on something of a rival.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan rejects Ibn Atiyya's construction: unlike ظن, أعطى cannot take أن and its clause as a substitute for its two objects.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba explains the word for discernment as specifying knowledge to a thing, and takes تعلمون to mean تعقلون, understanding.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس وقتادة ومقاتل | reports | Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Muqatil understand the omitted knowledge as awareness that God made the heavens, sent down water and performed the acts just described.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | A second interpretation attributed to Ibn Abbas is that the matter was not stated in the Torah and Gospel.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid takes the implied knowledge to be that God has no rival.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي بن عبيد الله | reports | Ali ibn Ubayd Allah says they know that no one else can perform the acts God has just described.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p162/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو محمد بن الخشاب | reports | Abu Muhammad ibn al-Khashab interprets the implied knowledge as awareness that the idols are stones.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r13] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The rebuke targets people who claim knowledge: associating despite the proofs shows they lack sound knowledge and are like beasts.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r14] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī argues that all creatures, high and low, depend on heaven, earth, and water, so making any of them God's rival contradicts necessary knowledge.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r15] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The verse rebukes those who abandon the one capable of everything to worship what can do nothing.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r16] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | This decisive teaching is shared by all revealed laws and scriptures and is the foundation of reverence, humility, and submission.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r17] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī says the passage trains the servant to turn sincerely to God by disowning the self, surrendering, serving reverently, relying on God, and resting in Him.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | When asked who he was, the Prophet declined to identify himself and answered that they were from water.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Earth and heaven contribute to human constitution, and their roles in producing provision follow from that; naming them also encompasses their full extent.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | The Prophet said that whoever usurps even a span of land will have it encircle him from seven earths; no grading is stated.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Earth is mentioned before heaven because people's attention turns to what is below them before what is above.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The manifest proof of lordship persuaded most people, while their hesitation concerned messengership, so the passage follows lordship with a warning about the message.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The prohibition follows from both the command to worship and the reminder that God alone performs the acts just listed.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Using the name Allah in the rebuke suits the condemnation of treating another as divine.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | reports | Alternatively, the prohibition can answer the hoped-for taqwa: lā is then negative and the verb is subjunctive.

[BURSEVI:v1p58#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | Al-Malakut divides the distances among the Sudanese, white lands, Persians, and Arabs as 12,000, 8,000, 3,000, and 1,000 farsakhs respectively.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | Al-Malakut places the center of the inhabited earth at the Kaaba and the center of all earth, inhabited and barren, at Qubbat al-Ard, where seasons and day and night remain balanced.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · علي | reports | ʿAli explains the name earth by saying it consumes what lies in its interior.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم | reports | Another etymology says earth is called so because hooves and feet wear or tread upon it.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Making earth a bed means exposing some of it from water and giving it a middle firmness and softness fit for sitting and sleeping, like a spread carpet; this does not require a flat surface, since its great spherical form allows it to be spread.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو الليث | reports | The sky is what rises above and shades people, built as a dome; each heaven lies over another, and the edges of the lowest heaven adjoin the earth, according to Abu al-Layth.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The water is rain descending from heaven onto clouds and from them to earth, rejecting the claim that it comes from the sea.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التيسير | reports | Here fruits include all edible produce that grows from earth and trees, such as grains and fruit.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God grows produce through the water: its active force interacts with earth's receptive force, like a marriage of sky and earth yielding fruit as offspring.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#3/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Min is explanatory and rizq means food for people and fodder for their animals; these gifts should lead them to recognize God as creator and provider and affirm His oneness.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#3/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Andad is the plural of nidd, a counterpart: do not worship supposed equals along with God or call them His partners.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#3/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas warns against attributing protection to others with statements such as that without a certain person or the barking dog, harm or theft would have occurred.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#3/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet warns against saying law, since hypocrites said that those who stayed with them would not have died or been killed.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#3/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · السعدي | reports | Saʿdi's couplet says that honor and glory or abasement and bondage are known to come from God, not from people such as ʿAmr and Zayd.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#4/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | People know God created them, their predecessors, heaven, earth, and provision, whereas idols neither harm nor benefit; the knowledge makes worship of rivals indefensible.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#4/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The universal favor prompts a question at resurrection: if God says He did all this for you, what will you say you did for Him?
[BURSEVI:v1p58#4/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو الحسين النوري | reports | When al-Shibli's sermon on the terrors of resurrection made listeners weep, Abu al-Husayn al-Nuri said not to frighten them: the reckoning is two questions, whether one was for God and whom one served.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#4/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verse calls for sincere worship: abandon regard for all besides God and witness the creator of night and day.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#4/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · السعدي | reports | Saʿdi's couplet stresses that without the root of sincerity, one is deprived at the door of devotion.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#4/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In advice to Muʿadh, the Prophet says seven angels existed before the heavens and earth, one gatekeeper was assigned to each heaven, and the servant's deeds ascend from morning to evening, radiant and magnified.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#4/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The first heaven's gatekeeper refuses the deed and strikes its owner's face because the servant backbit people; the accompanying verse says the tongue is for gratitude, while backbiting makes one ungrateful to God.
[BURSEVI:v1p58#4/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The second heaven's gatekeeper rejects a good deed because its owner sought worldly display and prided himself over people in their gatherings.
[BURSEVI:v1p60#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | First, since God alone made people, the heavens, earth, and everything for them, they must not make rivals in worship.
[BURSEVI:v1p60#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Second, the heavens, earth, sun, and moon are means of sustenance, but God alone provides; do not turn these means into rivals or prostrate to sun and moon.
[BURSEVI:v1p60#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Third, every creature has a share in something, and the human share is love and knowledge of God; rival beloveds sever that share and lead to ruin, as 2:165 describes. | mentions 2:165

[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | الذي may be accusative as an adjective or apposition to ربكم, or detached with an implied verb of specification or praise; Abu al-Baqa’s analysis as object of تتقون is rejected as weak.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Earth’s sphericity does not conflict with its being a spread bed: a sphere is so large that each portion is like a flat surface for use.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Using جعل here after خلق earlier reflects the different context or simply varies the expression, as in the cited verse. | mentions 6:1
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو البقاء | rejects | Abu al-Baqa’s parsing of الذي as the object of تتقون is, in al-Alusi’s judgment, an unworthy and feeble analysis of the Qur’an.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | It may instead be nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject or as a subject whose predicate is فلا تجعلوا; the fāʾ can introduce a predicate after a past relative clause. | mentions 85:10
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash allows an overt noun to serve as the linking pronoun in the relative construction; an imperative can be predicate through the standard interpretive account.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Alusi rejects the still more far-fetched proposal that الذي begins a clause whose predicate is رزقا لكم, understood with an omitted يرزق.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | جعل can mean ‘turned into,’ taking two objects, or ‘brought into existence,’ with the second accusative as a circumstantial phrase meaning the earth was created spread out for people.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The earth is like a bed because people can sit and sleep on it: God raised parts above water and made its firmness intermediate between hardness and softness for easy use.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | A report from Ibn Abbas says the earth was created before heaven without being spread, then spread out after heaven’s creation; this makes the sense of transformation explicit.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Alusi rejects explaining the transformed state by comparison with the Flood as ignorance’s confused waves; such an account is not common knowledge required by the description.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p188/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | He takes heaven as the upper direction or clouds; identifying it with the specific celestial sphere is also possible given God's power.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p188/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | If the second min is partitive, some fruits remain ungrown; rizqan is a causal verbal noun for producing, and lakum is attached to rizq as its object.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p188/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alternatively, min explains the kind: provided sustenance is the object of produce, lakum qualifies it, and the fronted fruit phrase becomes circumstantial.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p188/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī and many others allow the explanatory phrase to precede what it explains; al-Durr al-Maṣūn's author and others disallow that order.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p188/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Treating min as initial-source by supplying an omitted mention of fruits, or glossing fruits as seeds, is strained and unhelpful.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p188/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The definite article on fruits can mark either the genus or exhaustive inclusion; taking min as extra would entail that every produced fruit is sustenance for people, which is false.
